question: A running blog charted the marathon world records since 1988, men's and women's. Women look about to overtake. Where's the trick?
answer: In the two scales. On one, the gap barely moves: 14 minutes in 1988, 11 in 2023, about a tenth of the time. In 1992 two physiologists in Nature drew straight lines through earlier records and forecast women would catch men by 1998. That early surge was catch-up, as women finally got races and coaching.
move: When a trend flattens, ask what was driving it before.
ask: When a gap seems to be closing, do I check it on one scale before predicting the meeting point?

scene.headline: Women will soon outrun men
scene.honest: The gap: about a tenth, for 35 years
scene.label: Marathon world record, minutes
scene.found: Yes: men and women are drawn on different scales.
scene.miss: That part is fair. Compare the numbers on the two sides.

misses.headline: That's the forecast to test. The drawing is what sells it.
misses.marks: Each line is right for its own axis. Do they share one?

scene.name: Two scales, one race
scene.lesson: Two scales can make any gap close. Put both lines on one axis before believing a catch-up.

source: Whipp & Ward, Nature, 1992; Seiler et al., 2007
reference: Whipp & Ward, Will women soon outrun men?, Nature 355:25, 1992; Seiler, De Koning & Foster, The Fall and Rise of the Gender Difference in Elite Anaerobic Performance 1952–2006, Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2007; World Athletics marathon world record progression
